title: The Farewell Pilgrimage
teaser: He told the largest crowd he had ever faced that he did not know if he would stand there again.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A quiet warning given to one man first
layers.content:
The work was finished. Arabia had come over, the idols were down, and the man who had spent twenty years at it began to speak like someone with a departure date.

He said it first to one person. Sending Mu'adh bin Jabal to Yemen in the tenth year of the Hijra, he told him: O Mu'adh, you may not see me after this year. You may even pass by this very Masjid of mine and my grave. Mu'adh wept at the thought of being parted from him.

By then the pilgrimage season had turned Madinah into a kind of court. Representatives of the Arab tribes from the country around Makkah would gather at his door to consult him and to learn the laws and legislation of Islam, and he in turn would take their testimony — that he had delivered the trust, communicated the Message, and counselled the people. That year he announced that he would make the Hajj himself.

The town filled with people. Enormous crowds came into Madinah, all of them wanting to be led through the rites by him.

On a Saturday in the last four days of Dhul-Qa'dah he began his preparations. He combed his hair, applied perfume, put on his garments, saddled his camel, and set off in the afternoon. He reached Dhul-Hulaifah before the Asr prayer, prayed two units, and spent the night there.

In the morning he told his Companions what had happened while they slept. Someone, sent by my Lord, has called on me tonight and said: pray in this blessed valley, and say — I intend Umrah combined with Hajj.

Nobody riding with him knew that the journey would acquire a name. It is called Hajjatul-Wada', the Farewell Pilgrimage.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the night at Dhul-Hulaifah and the intention of Umrah combined with Hajj
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Eight Days to Makkah
layers.subtitle: Perfume left unwashed, and one instruction reversed
layers.content:
Before the Dhuhr prayer he bathed for ihram. Aishah applied perfume to his body and head with her own hands — Dharirah, a plant, and a scent containing musk. The thick sticky layer of it could be seen in his hair and his beard. He left it unwashed and put on his ihram clothing.

He shortened Dhuhr and prayed it as two units. Still standing at his prayer-place he proclaimed that he was performing Hajj associated with Umrah, and said: Labbaik, Allahumma Labbaik. I am at Your service, O Allah, I am at Your service. He mounted al-Qaswa' and said it again. When the open field came up around him, he said it again.

The column spent the last night at Dhi Tuwa. After the Fajr prayer he bathed, and entered Makkah on a Sunday morning, the fourth of Dhul-Hijjah. He had been eight days on the road, which was an average period for that distance.

He went into al-Masjid al-Haram, circumambulated the Ka'bah, and walked to and fro between Safa and Marwah. He did not leave ihram afterwards, because he was performing Qiran — Umrah and Hajj held together — and had brought his sacrificial animals with him. Then he camped at al-Hajun, on high ground above the city, and performed no further circuit until the circuit of the Hajj itself.

Those of his Companions who had brought no animals to sacrifice were ordered to convert their ihram into Umrah, circle the Ka'bah, walk between Safa and Marwah, and then come out of the sacred state. They showed reluctance to do it. He did not argue the point down. He said: had I known beforehand what I came to know later, I would not have brought the sacrificial animals with me, and if I did not have them, I would have come out of it too. On hearing that, they obeyed.

On the eighth, the Day of Tarwiyah, he went out to Mina and prayed all five prayers there. He waited until the sun rose on the ninth, then rode to Arafat, where a tent had been pitched for him at Namirah.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the ihram, the entry into Makkah on the fourth of Dhul-Hijjah, and the order to convert the ihram
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Sermon at Arafat
layers.subtitle: He said he might not stand there again
layers.content:
He sat inside the tent until the sun declined from its zenith. Then he ordered al-Qaswa' to be saddled, and rode down into the valley.

The gathering that formed around him is among the largest in the sirah, and the reports do not agree on its size: a hundred and twenty-four thousand, or a hundred and forty-four thousand. Rabi'ah bin Umaiyah bin Khalaf stood and repeated each sentence at full voice so the far edges of the crowd could hear it.

He opened with the reason they should listen. O people, listen to what I have to say, for I do not know whether I will ever meet you at this place after this year. Your blood, your property and your honour are as sacred as this day, this month, and this city.

Then he took the old order apart, item by item, and each time the first cut came out of his own household. All practices of paganism and ignorance, he said, are now under my feet. The blood revenge of the days of ignorance is remitted — and the first claim of blood he abolished was one owed within his own kin, that of Ibn Rabi'ah bin Harith, whom Hudhail killed. Usury is forbidden, he said, and I make a beginning by remitting the interest which Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib has to receive. His uncle's money went first.

People, fear Allah concerning your women. They have been taken on the security of Allah, he said; if they keep faith with you, clothe and feed them suitably.

Then the two sentences the whole speech was built to carry. Verily, I have left among you the Book of Allah — if you hold fast to it, you shall never go astray. And: O people, I am not succeeded by a Prophet, and you are not succeeded by any nation.

At the end he cross-examined them. When you are asked about me, what will you say? They answered: we bear witness that you have conveyed the Message and fulfilled your mission. He raised his forefinger to the sky, then brought it down toward them. O Allah, bear witness. He said it three times.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim — the sermon at Arafat; Ibn Hisham for Rabi'ah bin Umaiyah relaying the words aloud
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: Good news that one man heard as a loss
layers.content:
As soon as he finished the speech, a verse came down on him where he stood.

«الْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ الْإِسْلَامَ دِينًا» — 'This day I have perfected your religion for you, completed My Favour upon you, and have chosen for you Islam as your religion.' (5:3)

Umar bin al-Khattab heard it and began to cry. He was asked what made him weep. He said: nothing succeeds perfection but imperfection.

That is the whole of the reaction the sources preserve, and it is worth sitting with. The verse announced that the religion was complete. Umar heard in the same words that the man who had carried it was finished.

Bilal then made the announcement for the prayer, and then the second announcement, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed Dhuhr. Bilal pronounced the iqamah again immediately and he prayed Asr. No prayer was performed between the two. He mounted al-Qaswa', moved to the place of his standing, turned his face toward the qiblah, and stayed in that position until sunset — until the yellow had gone a little from the sky and the disc of the sun had disappeared.

A second revelation of that same pilgrimage said the same thing in a quieter register. Surat An-Nasr came down during the Days of Tashreeq at Mina: «إِذَا جَاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ وَالْفَتْحُ» — 'When the help of Allah comes, and the victory.' (110:1) al-Mubarakpuri records that when it was revealed to him he understood it as the announcement of his approaching death.

So the two revelations of that week did opposite work. One closed the religion. One closed the life. They came down within days of each other, on the same pilgrimage, in front of the same crowd.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim — the two prayers at Arafat with two iqamahs and no prayer between them
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: A route walked once and walked ever since
layers.content:
After sunset he took Usamah up behind him and rode to Muzdalifah, prayed Maghrib and Isha with one adhan and two iqamahs, and lay down until Fajr. In the morning he stopped at al-Mash'ar al-Haram to supplicate. Then on to Mina, with Fazal bin Abbas behind him, where he hurled seven small pebbles at the Big Jamrah, saying Allah is the Most Great at each one.

At the sacrificial place he slaughtered sixty-three camels with his own hands, then asked Ali to slaughter the remaining thirty-seven, making a hundred. A piece of meat from every animal was cooked in one pot, and the two men ate from it and drank the broth.

He rode back for the Tawaf al-Ifadah and prayed Dhuhr in Makkah, then went to Banu Abdul-Muttalib, who were drawing water for pilgrims at Zamzam: draw water, O Banu Abdul-Muttalib. I would have drawn it with you if I were not afraid that after me people would rush to take this honour from you.

He preached again late that morning, mounted on a grey mule, Ali carrying his words out to the crowd. What month is this? What is this town called? What day is this? Each time they said Allah and His Messenger know best; each time he waited, then named it — Dhul-Hijjah, al-Baldah, the Day of Slaughter — and set their blood, property and honour beside it as equally sacred. Then: have I not delivered the Message of my Lord? They said, yes, you have. O Allah, bear witness. Let him that is present convey it to him who is absent, for to whom the message is conveyed may have more understanding of it than the audience.

He spent the days of Tashreeq at Mina, teaching. On the thirteenth he left, slept a few hours at al-Abtah, then performed the Farewell Circumambulation and ordered his Companions to do the same. Then he turned north — not, al-Mubarakpuri writes, to seek rest, but to resume the struggle.

Carry this. Every pilgrim since has walked that week in that order because he walked it once. And he did not close it by asking to be admired. He closed it by asking to be passed on.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the rites from Muzdalifah to the Farewell Circumambulation, and the sermon on the Day of Slaughter
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say to Mu'adh bin Jabal when sending him to Yemen in the tenth year of the Hijra?

options.text: That Yemen would be the last land to accept Islam
That Mu'adh might not see him after that year, and might pass by his Masjid and his grave
That he should return before the pilgrimage season
That he was to collect the poor-due and bring it to Madinah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Symptoms of Farewell, and the dispatch of Mu'adh to Yemen
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar treats this as the earliest of the signals. Mu'adh wept on hearing it. The word 'grave' was in the sentence, and Mu'adh understood exactly what he had been told.

quiz.prompt: How many people are reported to have gathered around him in the valley at Arafat?

options.text: Ten thousand, the same number that marched on Makkah
Exactly one hundred thousand, agreed by every narration
Reports differ — a hundred and twenty-four thousand, or a hundred and forty-four thousand
Thirty thousand, the size of the army at Tabuk

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Farewell Pilgrimage, on the gathering at Arafat
quiz.scholar_reflection: The sources give two figures and do not reconcile them. What both agree on is the scale: this was the largest audience he ever addressed, and a man had to be posted to relay his sentences to the edges of it.

quiz.prompt: When he abolished usury in the sermon, whose interest payment did he cancel first?

options.text: That owed to the Jewish lenders of Madinah
That owed to Abu Sufyan, as a condition of his Islam
That owed to the poor among the Emigrants
That owed to his own uncle, Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the sermon at Arafat, quoting the abolition of usury
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did the same thing twice in one paragraph. The first blood claim he cancelled was one owed inside his own kin; the first interest he cancelled was his uncle's income. The reform began where it cost him.

quiz.prompt: Which verse was revealed to him immediately after he finished the sermon at Arafat?

options.text: 'This day I have perfected your religion for you' (5:3)
'When the help of Allah comes, and the victory' (110:1)
'So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram' (2:144)
'Muhammad is no more than a Messenger' (3:144)

quiz.citation: Quran 5:3 — al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, on the revelation following the sermon
quiz.scholar_reflection: Surat An-Nasr also came down on this pilgrimage, but later, during the Days of Tashreeq at Mina. The verse at Arafat was the one about perfection, and Umar wept at it.

quiz.prompt: One hundred camels were sacrificed. How was that divided?

options.text: All hundred were slaughtered by the Companions on his instruction
He slaughtered sixty-three with his own hands and Ali slaughtered the other thirty-seven
They were distributed among the tribes to slaughter in their own camps
Ali slaughtered all of them while the Prophet ﷺ recited

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Day of Slaughter at Mina
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was sixty-three years old. The number he cut with his own hands matched his years, and Ali completed the hundred. Meat from every one of the hundred went into a single pot, and the two men ate from it together.

quiz.prompt: He opened the sermon by saying he did not know whether he would ever meet them in that place again. What does that do to the sentences that follow it?

options.text: It strips out anything decorative — only what matters gets said
It makes the crowd listen differently, which was part of the point
It is a hard way to begin, and I would avoid saying it
It puts the weight of transmission on them, not on him

quiz.slider_label: Spare them the warning — Tell them plainly
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the opening of the sermon at Arafat
quiz.scholar_reflection: Read the sermon back with that first line in mind. There is no preamble, no self-defence, and almost no narrative. It is a list of obligations, and then a demand that they be carried out of the valley.

quiz.prompt: Umar heard 'This day I have perfected your religion for you' and wept, saying nothing succeeds perfection but imperfection. Have you ever received good news and felt what it was ending?

options.text: Yes — arriving somewhere always means leaving the road behind
He was reading grief into a verse of pure mercy
He knew the man better than the words, and heard the man in them
Completion frightens me more than difficulty does

quiz.slider_label: A gift completed — A door closing
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Rahmatul-lil-'Alamin — Umar's weeping at the revelation of 5:3
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nobody else in the account cried. The verse was heard as good news by the crowd and as a bereavement notice by one man standing in it. Both readings were correct.

quiz.prompt: At Zamzam he declined to draw water alongside Banu Abdul-Muttalib, saying he feared that after him people would rush to take the honour from them. What is he protecting?

options.text: A family's inherited office from being seized by imitation
The principle that his own example creates obligations he must weigh
Nothing much — it reads as tribal favour to his own clan
The pilgrims, who need the water more than they need a symbol

quiz.slider_label: Join the work — Guard their office
quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — at the well of Zamzam
quiz.scholar_reflection: He accepted the water and drank from it. What he refused was to be seen doing the job, because he understood that anything he did once would be copied by thousands, and the copying would displace the family that had held the duty.

quiz.prompt: He ended by saying: let him that is present convey it to him who is absent, for the one it reaches may understand it better than the audience. How do you read that last clause?

options.text: Proximity to a teacher is no guarantee of understanding him
It is a warning to the first generation not to hoard authority
It puts the far-off reader on level ground with the eyewitness
It is mainly an instruction to transmit accurately, whatever I make of it

quiz.slider_label: The witnesses knew best — The distant may know better
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari — the sermon on the Day of Slaughter, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was speaking to more than a hundred thousand people who had walked days to hear him, and he told them the message might land deeper somewhere they would never see. That sentence is why the sermon survived.

quiz.prompt: After the Farewell Circumambulation he went back to Madinah — al-Mubarakpuri writes, not to seek rest but to resume the struggle. He had roughly three months left. What do you make of that choice?

options.text: He did not know the timing, so there was nothing to change
The signals suggest he half knew, and worked anyway
Work was the only form his farewell could take
I would have spent those months differently, and I am not sure that is wrong

quiz.slider_label: Rest at the end — Work to the end
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the return to Madinah after the Farewell Pilgrimage
quiz.scholar_reflection: Within weeks of the return he was mobilising an army under Usamah bin Zaid for the Byzantine frontier. The pilgrimage was the summing-up. It was not a retirement.
